questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating an Exponential Function with a Linear Exponent
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=-4{e}^{u},\,u=2-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-4{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-4{e}^{u}\cdot (-1) \\  & =4{e}^{u} \\  & =4{e}^{2-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=2-ln⁡(3)$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=2-ln⁡(3)} & =4{e}^{2-(2-ln⁡(3))} \\  & =4{e}^{ln⁡(3)} \\  & =4\cdot 3 \\  & =12.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=-3{e}^{u},\,u=5-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=-3{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =-3{e}^{u}\cdot (-1) \\  & =3{e}^{u} \\  & =3{e}^{5-x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=5-ln⁡(2)$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=5-ln⁡(2)} & =3{e}^{5-(5-ln⁡(2))} \\  & =3{e}^{ln⁡(2)} \\  & =3\cdot 2 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent to the curve $y=5{e}^{4x}$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y=5{e}^{u},\,u=4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=5{e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =5{e}^{u}\cdot 4 \\  & =20{e}^{u} \\  & =20{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{1}{4}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1/4} & ={(20{e}^{4x})|}_{x=1/4} \\  & =20{e}^{4(1/4)} \\  & =20e\end{aligned}
$$

Also, the $y$-value of the point on the curve where $x={x}_{1}=\frac{1}{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & ={(5{e}^{4x})|}_{x=1/4} \\  & =5{e}^{4(1/4)} \\  & =5e.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we find the equation of the tangent at that point:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5e & =20e(x-\frac{1}{4}) \\ y-5e & =20ex-5e \\ y & =20ex\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y={e}^{-3x+5}$ as the composite function

$$
y={e}^{u},\,u=-3x+5.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-3.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (-3) \\  & =-3{e}^{u} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3x+5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the sum rule of differentiation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(8x+{e}^{-3x+5}) \\  & =8-3{e}^{-3x+5} \\  & =-3{e}^{-3x+5}+8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={e}^{{x}^{3}-4x}$ at the point where $x=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={e}^{u},\,u={x}^{3}-4x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={e}^{u},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}-4.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (3{x}^{2}-4) \\  & =(3{x}^{2}-4){e}^{{x}^{3}-4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=2$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=2} & ={(3{x}^{2}-4){e}^{{x}^{3}-4x}\,|}_{x=2} \\  & =(3(2)^{2}-4){e}^{{2}^{3}-4(2)} \\  & =8\cdot {e}^{0} \\  & =8\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a General Exponential Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={5}^{u},\,u=x-{x}^{3}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={5}^{u}ln⁡(5),\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1-3{x}^{2}.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={5}^{u}ln⁡(5)\cdot (1-3{x}^{2}) \\  & =(1-3{x}^{2}){5}^{x-{x}^{3}}ln⁡(5).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope $m$ of the tangent to the curve at $x=1$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}m={\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={((1-3{x}^{2}){5}^{x-{x}^{3}}ln⁡(5))|}_{x=1} \\  & =(1-3(1)^{2}){5}^{1-(1)^{3}}ln⁡(5) \\  & =-2\cdot {5}^{0}ln⁡(5) \\  & =-2ln⁡(5)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={4}^{7x}$ at the point where $x=\frac{1}{7}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={4}^{u},\,u=7x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}={4}^{u}ln⁡4,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=7.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={4}^{u}ln⁡4\cdot 7 \\  & =7ln⁡4\cdot {4}^{u} \\  & =7ln⁡4\cdot {4}^{7x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{1}{7}$, we have to evaluate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ at that point as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{x=1/7} & =7ln⁡(4)\cdot {4}^{7(1/7)} \\  & =7ln⁡(4)\cdot 4 \\  & =28ln⁡(4)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $x=\frac{1}{7}$ is $28ln⁡(4).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating an Exponential Function with a Linear Exponent
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $f(x)$ as the composite function

$$
f = e^u, \qquad u=5x+4.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d u} = e^u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =5.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot 5 \\  & =5{e}^{u} \\  & =5{e}^{5x+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $y=e^{-x^2},$ calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = e^u, \qquad u=-x^2.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = e^u,\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =-2x.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{u}\cdot (-2x) \\  & =-2x{e}^{u} \\  & =-2x{e}^{-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $y= 3\cdot 2^{1 - x},$ find $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y = 3\cdot 2^u, \qquad u=1-x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d u} = 3\cdot 2^u\ln(2),\qquad \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x} =-1.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{u}ln⁡(2)\cdot (-1) \\  & =-3\cdot {2}^{u}ln⁡(2) \\  & =-3\cdot {2}^{1-x}ln⁡(2).\end{aligned}
$$
